Newly hatched chicks of the Two-barred crossbill emerge after an incubation period of 13 days [ab = 13 days] at 32 °C [T = 32 °C] and possess an initial wet body mass averaging 2.54 grams [Ww0 = 2.54 grams]. This modest starting weight, typical of small-bodied cardueline finches, marks the beginning of a rapid developmental trajectory that is tightly coupled to the seasonal abundance of conifer seeds. Field observations indicate that at this same incubation temperature, the nestlings achieve nutritional independence and fledge from the nest at 21 days after hatching [tx = 21 days after hatching], a period that allows sufficient time for feather development and the acquisition of basic foraging skills before the parents cease provisioning at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The relatively short nestling phase is an adaptation to the unpredictable availability of spruce and pine cones, which can fluctuate dramatically from year to year.

Under the thermal conditions typical of the species' active metabolic regime, measured at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum lifespan of the Two-barred crossbill reaches approximately 4 years [am = approximately 4 years]. This relatively brief longevity, compared to other finches of similar body size, reflects the high energetic demands of a nomadically foraging lifestyle in boreal and subarctic environments. Studies based on recapture data from banding programs suggest that most individuals do not survive beyond their third winter, with predation, food scarcity, and severe weather acting as the primary agents of mortality. The species' life history strategy thus emphasizes early and rapid reproduction over extended somatic persistence.

Sexual maturation in the Two-barred crossbill occurs relatively early for a bird of its body size, with gonadal development completing at 63 days after hatching [tp = 63 days after hatching] at the standard active temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This rapid progression to reproductive capability is a critical adaptation for exploiting ephemeral cone crops, allowing young-of-the-year to breed during the same summer in which they were hatched if food resources are sufficiently abundant. The maturation of the reproductive tract is tightly synchronized with photoperiod and food availability, and males typically develop their characteristically crossed mandibles before attempting to court potential mates. The timing of puberty is thus a key determinant of the species' ability to irruptively colonize new areas.

The age at which Two-barred crossbills produce their first brood is 0.92 years since birth [tR = 0.92 years since birth], measured under the 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] thermal conditions that characterize their summer breeding season. This early onset of reproduction is a hallmark of the species' opportunistic life history, enabling them to capitalize on bumper cone crops that may occur only once every several years. Females construct nests in coniferous trees, lining them with fine grasses and feathers to provide insulation for the eggs and subsequent altricial young. The first successful nesting attempt often occurs within the first calendar year, a strategy that maximizes lifetime reproductive output despite a potentially short adult lifespan.

Adult females of the Two-barred crossbill attain an ultimate wet body mass of 32.7 grams [Wwi = 32.7 grams], while adult males are slightly lighter at 30.45 grams [Wwi = 30.45 grams]. This moderate sexual size dimorphism, with females being the larger sex, is relatively uncommon among cardueline finches and may relate to the energetic demands of egg production and incubation. The combination of a small initial mass and a female asymptotic weight that is over twelve times greater than the neonatal mass underscores the intensity of the growth period. In terms of reproductive output, females produce two eggs per clutch [N_R_i = two eggs per clutch], and typically raise one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year] during irruption years, with the basal metabolic rate of adults measured at 83.5 milliliters per hour [JOi = 83.5 milliliters per hour] when maintained at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C].
